final.regime_evidence: The Federal Reserve initiated a rate-hiking cycle on March 16 [D03], and CPI inflation reached 7.9% in February [D02], signaling a significant shift away from the cheap-funding environment that supported growth and venture-style assets [D01].
final.book_exposure: The portfolio carries significant exposure to long-duration assets, including public growth equities, venture holdings, and SPACs, which are disproportionately sensitive to rising discount rates [D01].
actions: Reduce exposure to high-multiple growth equities and speculative SPACs to limit sensitivity to rising discount rates [D01].
Exit illiquid private assets reliant on cheap funding [D01].
Reduce overall gross exposure to improve liquidity and risk positioning in the new rates regime [D05].
final.target_gross_net: Lower gross and net exposure significantly to align with a defensive posture during a regime change.

drivers.driver: The transition from a low-rate regime to a tightening cycle specifically targets the duration and valuation of growth, venture, and SPAC holdings [D01].
Shrinking liquidity and higher discount rates undermine the funding models of cash-burning growth companies [D05].
The portfolio's heavy skew toward long-duration equities necessitates a reduction in gross risk to preserve capital and prevent forced selling [D08].
The shift in macro regime—marked by the first rate hike and persistent inflation—renders previous valuation multiples for growth assets unsustainable [D02].

final.memo:
The regime has decisively changed. We are moving from an era of easy money to a cycle of persistent inflation and rising policy rates [D03]. Our portfolio, heavily weighted toward long-duration growth, venture, and SPAC-related risk, is poorly positioned for this pivot. As we noted in our February discussions, private markets reliant on cheap funding face inevitable revaluation [D01]. 

We must act quickly to reduce gross exposure. Staying committed to growth names solely because of brand quality or historical performance is a dangerous error when the underlying cost of capital has moved upward [D05]. We are cutting back on these speculative exposures to harden the book and preserve liquidity, prioritizing companies with genuine cash generation over those dependent on external funding rounds [D01]. This is not a time to wait for a rebound; it is a time to prune the portfolio of assets whose economics are anchored to a liquidity environment that no longer exists [D05].
